fr:title.text: Risks and Open Questions — Derivative-Based CFG Parser

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Risks and Open Questions — Derivative-Based CFG Parser

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Risks for the plan, ordered by how likely they are to cause rework.

html:ul.html:li: Productivity of μ in CFGDesc. The non-nullable-prefix condition is the natural guardedness criterion, but formalising it compositionally (so all constructors preserve it with reasonable evidence) is not obvious. A too-strict condition rules out Dyck; a too-loose one fails to give well-founded derivatives.

Derivative descriptions on μ. Unfolding under δ is the standard trick, but in a strongly-typed setting we have to show that the unfolded description is again a legal CFGDesc (productivity preserved). Might need to enrich CFGDesc with a rec or ν constructor that tracks the "unfolded state".

Nullability gate interacting with ⟜. The Brzozowski rule δ c (G · H) = δ c G · H ⊕ ν? G · δ c H uses classical disjunction. In Lambek we need the grammar-level iso c · (G · H) ≅ (c · G) · H + [G is ε-derivable] · (c · H); the second summand is zero when G is non-nullable. Check that the ⟜-as-derivative framing still composes cleanly through this case distinction.

c2a-morph at Type vs Set. The intrinsically-recursive paper is formalised in Set^I. Grammars in this project are String → Type. The constructions look generic over the universe, but there may be isSet obligations (or propositional-truncation issues) hidden in the uniqueness proof. See parser as c2a-morphism.

Infinite state space. For CFGs the reachable derivatives of a grammar are unbounded. We don't need finitely many descriptions, but we do need each derivative to be well-typed and computable. The danger is that our description type is not closed under δ — i.e., δ produces something outside CFGDesc. This has to be proven, not just asserted.

Coalgebraic "parsing" framing vs Parser record. Cass's Automata.Deterministic.parseNatTrans is a natural transformation between the word functor and the trace functor — a genuine coalgebraic object — but it gives a DFA-shaped coalgebra that doesn't obviously subsume our Parser A B return type. We may need to compose their NT-style result with a decide step on the final state to recover A ⊕ B. Not blocking, but a loose end.

Constructive negation of CFG. ¬ ⟦ G ⟧cfg w is what Parser wants on the reject side, but in general the negation of a CFG membership predicate is not itself a CFG. We will be inhabiting a proof of non-membership, not a grammar. Worth confirming that the disjointness obligation disjoint A B is satisfied by this formulation.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Validation milestone: implement hand-rolled Dyck parser end-to-end, before generalising to CFGDesc. Concrete failure modes surface much faster at the semantic level.

fr:title.text: The guard makes δ total: derivative parsing for the guarded CFG fragment

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The guard makes δ total: derivative parsing for the guarded CFG fragment

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Claim. If we restrict parsing-with-derivatives to the guarded (productive) grammar fragment — the same well-formedness condition of sss-00AC that we already impose to make recursive grammar definitions meaningful — then the two things that make parsing-with-derivatives hard for general context-free grammars both disappear, and the derivative becomes an ordinary total, structurally-defined operation. This tree spells out why, because the reason is not obvious and is the whole basis for the feasibility claim.

Throughout, ε is the grammar matching only the empty string (the tensor unit), ⊥ the grammar matching nothing, · concatenation, ⊕ alternation, A* Kleene star, and char a the single-character grammar. δ c G is the syntactic derivative and ν? G the nullability gate (ν? G = ε if G accepts the empty string, else ⊥).

fr:title.text: Background: what parsing-with-derivatives does, and why general CFGs are hard

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Background: what parsing-with-derivatives does, and why general CFGs are hard

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The Brzozowski derivative δ c G is "G, assuming the first character c has already been read": it is a proof-relevant iso (δ c G) w ≅ G (c ∷ w) (sss-00A7), so it transports parse trees, not just acceptance. Parsing is then a fold over the input — one derivative per character — that at the end reads off the empty-string parse trees of the residual and reshapes them back through the derivative isos into a parse of the whole input (the full construction, and why it is a genuine tree-producing parser rather than a recognizer, is sss-00F0):

html:p.html:code: parse G (c ∷ w) = deriv⁻¹ (parse (δ c G) w)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Here ν? below is only the nullability gate inside δ's definition (does the empty-string part exist), not the output.
The derivative is computed by pushing δ c through the grammar structure. The two rules that recurse into subgrammars are the ones to watch:

html:p.html:code: δ c (A ⊕ B) = δ c A ⊕ δ c B
δ c (A · B) = δ c A · B ⊕ ν? A · δ c B

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The product rule is the subtle one. Differentiating a concatenation A · B has two cases: either the first character came from A (giving δ c A · B), or A could match the empty string and the first character came from B (giving δ c B, but only if A is nullable — hence the ν? A gate).
Where general CFGs break. For a recursive grammar the derivative can refer back to itself. Take the left-recursive E = (E · char a) ⊕ char b. Differentiating:

html:p.html:code: δ a E = δ a (E · char a) ⊕ δ a (char b) = (δ a E · char a ⊕ ν? E · δ a (char a)) ⊕ ⊥

fr:mainmatter.html:p: which is an equation defining δ a E in terms of δ a E. There is no structural computation here: δ a E can only be obtained as the least fixed point of that equation. This is exactly why the classical functional-pearl implementation (Might–Darais–Spiewak 2011) needs laziness, observable sharing, and memoized fixed points — and why nullability there is also a least-fixed-point computation. Both difficulties come from a nonterminal being reachable by δ without any character being consumed first.

fr:title.text: The keystone: guardedness cuts every self-differentiation branch

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: The keystone: guardedness cuts every self-differentiation branch

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A grammar is guarded when, in every production, each nonterminal occurrence is preceded by a non-nullable prefix — you cannot reach the nonterminal without first consuming at least one terminal. (E above is not guarded: its recursive E is the leading factor, preceded by nothing.)

Keystone Lemma. On the guarded fragment, δ c is a total function definable by structural recursion, computed with one unfolding of each fixed point and no auxiliary fixed point or memoization; moreover it sends guarded grammars to guarded grammars.

Why. The only way δ c fails to terminate structurally is if computing δ c X for a nonterminal X requires computing δ c X again — the cyclic equation we saw for E. That happens iff δ c can descend to a differentiated occurrence of X, i.e. iff X is reachable in the production body without passing a consuming prefix. Guardedness forbids exactly this. Consider where a guarded X sits: behind a non-nullable prefix A, as A · (⋯X⋯). The product rule splits differentiation of A · (⋯X⋯) into two branches:

html:ul.html:li: δ c A · (⋯X⋯) — keeps the X-containing tail unchanged, so X is carried along as an undifferentiated leaf; and
ν? A · δ c (⋯X⋯) — the branch that would recurse toward δ c X, but A is non-nullable, so ν? A = ⊥ and this whole branch is ⊥.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: So δ c reaches every nonterminal only through the first branch, as a leaf it does not differentiate. Concretely, computing δ c X for a guarded X unfolds X's body once and makes a single structural pass, treating every nonterminal in the body (recursive or not) as an opaque leaf, because each is guarded and its ν?-gate is ⊥. The pass therefore calls δ c on no nonterminal at all — it cannot diverge, and it cannot form a cycle (even a mutual one). The output is a finite expression over the original nonterminals. ∎

The contrast with E: for E the recursive occurrence has an empty (hence nullable) prefix, so the ν? A gate is ε rather than ⊥, the second branch survives, and δ a E is forced to recurse into δ a E. The guard is precisely the syntactic condition that keeps that gate shut.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Worked example: aⁿbⁿ (guarded, not regular)

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Let S = (char a · S · char b) ⊕ ε. The recursive S is guarded — it sits behind the non-nullable char a. First derivative:

html:p.html:code: δ a S = δ a (char a · (S · char b)) ⊕ δ a ε
= [ δ a (char a) · (S · char b) ⊕ ν?(char a) · δ a (S · char b) ] ⊕ ⊥
= [ ε · (S · char b) ⊕ ⊥ · δ a (S · char b) ] ⊕ ⊥

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Notice the second branch ν?(char a) · δ a (S · char b) became ⊥ because ν?(char a) = ⊥. This is the gate closing: we never had to compute δ a (S · char b), so the computation of δ a S terminates in one unfold, and the result S · char b carries the original S undifferentiated.
Now a residual like S · char b does have S as its leading factor, so its own derivative genuinely calls δ a S:

html:p.html:code: δ a (S · char b) = δ a S · char b ⊕ ν? S · δ a (char b) = (S · char b) · char b ⊕ (ε · ⊥) = S · char b · char b

fr:mainmatter.html:p: But δ a S here is just the terminating one-unfold computation above (= S · char b), so there is no infinite regress — only a finite chain of residuals S, S · char b, S · char b · char b, …, each a finite expression over the original S. The state space is infinite (this grammar is not regular), but see below: that never matters for a single parse.

fr:title.text: Nullability collapses for the same reason

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Nullability collapses for the same reason

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For general CFGs, ν? is itself a least fixed point: whether a nonterminal is nullable can depend recursively on whether it is nullable. The guard removes this too, by the identical mechanism. A guarded recursive occurrence sits behind a non-nullable prefix, and
ν?(char a · X) = ν?(char a) · ν? X = ⊥ · ν? X = ⊥, for any X.

So a production containing a guarded recursive occurrence is non-nullable outright, regardless of the occurrence's own nullability — the recursive dependency is severed. Nullability of μX. F is then determined entirely by the non-recursive (base) alternatives of F, computable by structural recursion with no iteration to a fixed point. For aⁿbⁿ:
ν? S = ν?(char a · S · char b) ⊕ ν? ε = ⊥ ⊕ ε = ε (nullable, via the ε branch), computed without ever consulting ν? S.
This is why sss-00A5 is clean on the guarded fragment, and the same ν?-computation doubles as the check that a grammar really is guarded.

fr:title.text: What does not collapse — and why it is harmless

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: What does not collapse — and why it is harmless

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Infinitely many derivatives. As the aⁿbⁿ example shows, a guarded (indeed any non-regular) grammar has infinitely many distinct derivative states, so there is no finite derivative automaton to precompute. This sounds alarming but is irrelevant to actually parsing: parsing a fixed input w takes exactly |w| derivative steps, each a total finite operation, and the parser is structurally recursive on the input list. You never enumerate the state space; you only ever walk one path of length |w| through it. (This is the same observation sss-00A6 makes as "infinite but regular-in-the-right-sense".)

Description blow-up. The product rule duplicates subgrammars — δ c (A · B) mentions B in one branch and δ c B in the other — so a naively-represented residual can grow exponentially in |w|. The remedy is compaction: algebraic simplification after each step (⊥ · x = ⊥, ε · x = x, x ⊕ ⊥ = x, and sharing of common nonterminals). The essential point for us is that compaction is an optimization, not a correctness requirement: a total, correct parser exists without it (each step is already total), so compaction and its semantics-preservation proof can be added later, purely for performance. This is the one place where the general-CFG performance story (cubic only with compaction, per Adams–Hollenbeck–Might 2016) still applies — but it is decoupled from totality and correctness.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Deliverables

fr:mainmatter.html:p: With the keystone lemma in hand the remaining work is small and well-scoped:

html:ol.html:li: Totality and guard-preservation of δ — formalize the keystone lemma: on the guarded fragment δ c is total, structural, and maps guarded grammars to guarded grammars. This discharges the "μ is the part most likely to need care" flag of sss-00A6 and the corresponding risk; the care needed is precisely the ν?-gate argument above.

The parser as a fold / Löb fixed point — the length-recursion parser of sss-00A8, parse G (c ∷ w) = deriv⁻¹ (parse (δ c G) w), producing parse trees by reshaping along the derivative iso, optionally recast as the (Brz) Löb fixed point of sss-00EY / sss-00EX for a modality-native presentation (the guarded recursion is exactly what Löb discharges). Its output is the parse forest ⟦G⟧ w, per sss-00F0.

Soundness and completeness are automatic — the derivative commutation ⟦ δ c G ⟧ ≅ ⟦ G ⟧ ⟜ char c of sss-00A7 is a proof-relevant iso, so the fold is the bijection ⟦G⟧ w ≅ ⟦δ_w G⟧ ε; there is no separate correctness proof, and parse trees / semantic actions ride along the isos. Because δ is structural, no fixed-point / domain-theoretic reasoning is needed.
(Optional) Compaction with preservation — for performance only: prove each simplification rule is a grammar isomorphism, so parse trees / semantic actions are preserved.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Precision: "guarded", not "non-left-recursive"

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The exact restriction is the ▷-guard of sss-00AC: every self-reference under a non-nullable prefix. This is strictly stronger than "not directly left-recursive". Consider hidden left recursion, A = (B · A) ⊕ c with B nullable: A is not the syntactic leading factor, but because B can vanish, A is still reachable with no character consumed, so ν? B = ε keeps the dangerous branch open and δ c A again becomes cyclic. Guardedness rules this out too — it is about consumption, not syntactic position. So state the fragment as guarded / productive.

fr:title.text: Parser as Unique c2a-Morphism of a Recursive Coalgebra

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Parser as Unique c2a-Morphism of a Recursive Coalgebra

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Goal: reinterpret the length-recursive parser as the unique coalgebra-to-algebra morphism produced by the c2a-morph construction of [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] (file IntrinsicallyRecursiveCoalgs.lagda, module c2a.c2a-morph).
Concretely we need to supply five pieces:

html:ol.html:li: A carrier C : ℕ → Type (indexed by input length). The coalgebra input at length n is the set of strings of that length paired with the current derivative state G.
A well-founded relation on ℕ: the standard _<_, with well-foundedness from Cubical.Induction.WellFounded.
A base endofunctor F on ℕ → Type expressing one character of progress: F X n = nullability-answer-at-0 ⊕ (Alphabet × X (n-1)).
The well-foundedness witness F-ε⁻¹ : F X n ⊢ (F ↓₀) X n coming from the fact that every recursive occurrence sits under a strictly-decreasing length.
A coalgebra c : C ⇒ F C (one step of derivative) and an algebra a : F Answer ⇒ Answer, where Answer G w = Parser ⟦ G ⟧cfg (¬ ⟦ G ⟧cfg) w.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Applying c2a.c2a-morph to these yields a morphism parse : C ⇒ Answer together with the uniqueness property inherited from the recursive-coalgebra framework. Uniqueness is exactly the statement that "the parser is the correct parser" — there is only one coalgebra-to-algebra morphism, so any alternative definition agrees with ours on every input.
Contrast with the intrinsically-recursive GCD and CYK:

html:ul.html:li: GCD is well-founded on proj₂ of ℕ × ℕ. Ours is well-founded on length of the string — the same idea (project down to ℕ, use <).

CYK uses List⁺ to sidestep nullability entirely. We cannot do that — nullability is a first-class question for CFGs — but we handle it by threading the nullability decision through the algebra at length 0.
Both GCD and CYK pay the price of defining the base functor and its well-foundedness lemma by hand. Ours pays the same price uniformly, parameterised over G : CFGDesc.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open: does c2a-morph give us extensional uniqueness (the thing we want, since grammars are propositions at each string), or does it give a stronger computational equality? IntrinsicallyRecursiveCoalgs proves unique.unique at the indexed-set level; check whether its use of Set-level equalities causes friction with our Type-valued grammars. Tracked in risks.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Linear Residual ⟜ as Brzozowski Derivative

fr:mainmatter.html:p: In Grammar.LinearFunction.Base, the right residual is (A ⟜ B) w = ∀ (w' : String) → B w' → A (w' ++ w). Reading this at a single-character grammar char c we get
(G ⟜ char c) w = ∀ w' → (char c) w' → G (w' ++ w) ≅ G (c ∷ w),
i.e. the Brzozowski derivative of G by c, up to the canonical iso char c · w ≅ c ∷ w for singleton matches.

So the calculus already has a semantic notion of derivative as a type constructor, not just as an operation on descriptions. The syntactic derivative δ c G should then denote exactly ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⟜ char c, and the Brzozowski adjointness c · G ≅ δ c G is an instance of the tensor/residual adjunction char c · G ⊢ H ⟺ G ⊢ H ⟜ char c.
Why this matters for the plan:

html:ul.html:li: It grounds δ in the calculus rather than treating it as an external device: δ c G = G ⟜ char c already has the right type.
It means the parser's recursive structure can be phrased internally as currying over char c · - / uncurrying over - ⟜ char c, without leaving the calculus.
It suggests CFGDesc may not need ⟜ as a primitive — the operator can live outside the description as long as we can compute δ on descriptions and prove ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg ≅ ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⟜ char c.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open question: for grammars with nullable residuals the adjunction interacts with the nullability gating in δ c (G · H); make sure the semantic direction of the iso stays available in both cases. This is tracked in risks.

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Syntactic Derivatives on CFGDesc

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Given a character c : Alphabet and a description G : CFGDesc, define a description δ c G : CFGDesc and a morphism at the semantics
deriv c G : char c · ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⊢ ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg ,
together with an inverse deriv⁻¹ c G : ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg ⊢ char c · ⟦ G ⟧cfg , so the pair witnesses the Brzozowski identity c · G ≅ δ c G inside grammar (not language) semantics.
Regex case is classical:

html:ul.html:li: δ c ε = ⊥;
δ c (char a) = if a ≟ c then ε else ⊥;
δ c (G · H) = (δ c G) · H ⊕ ν? G · δ c H, where ν? gates the second summand by nullability;
δ c (G ⊕ H) = δ c G ⊕ δ c H;
δ c (G *) = δ c G · G *.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: For μ we unfold once before deriving, using the productivity side condition to ensure the derivative terminates at the description level (the description does not grow under δ past a bounded residual form). This is the part most likely to need care — see risks.

CFG derivatives in general (Might, Darais, Spiewak 2011) form an infinite but regular-in-the-right-sense family; the reachable derivative states for a given G correspond to the states of a PDA for G. We do not need finitely many residuals; we only need each derivative to be well-typed and to decrease the string length we feed it.

For Dyck specifically, the derivative by LP moves us to a state "expecting one extra RP before completion", and iterating gives the unbounded stack. The state space is infinite; the per-string computation is still well-founded on input length, which is where well-founded recursion on length comes in.

fr:title.text: Plan: Derivative-Based CFG Parser via Recursive Coalgebras

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Plan: Derivative-Based CFG Parser via Recursive Coalgebras

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A concrete path for exercising well-founded recursive coalgebras in dep-Lambek: build a generic derivative-based parser for a syntactically-delimited class of context-free grammars, in direct analogy with the existing regular-expression infrastructure (Grammar.RegularExpression). Every step should admit a compositional, well-founded account, and the whole thing should ultimately factor through the c2a-morph theorem of [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint].

The Dyck language serves as the running test: it is not regular, its derivatives form an infinite (PDA-shaped) state space, and it cannot admit a map string ⊢ Dyck — only a Parser Dyck ¬Dyck. We want to derive the automaton shape, not assume it.
The phases:

html:ol.html:li: CFGDesc: an embedded syntax of guarded CFGs.
Decidable nullability for CFGDesc.
Syntactic derivatives on CFGDesc.
Linear residual ⟜ as Brzozowski derivative.
Parser by well-founded recursion on string length.
Parser as unique c2a-morphism of a recursive coalgebra.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Risks and open questions are tracked in sss-00AA.
An orthogonal re-foundation that would internalise phases 2 and 5 into the type system is discussed in Later operator ▶ as internalised guard.

First concrete deliverable: a hand-coded Dyck parser at the semantic level (outside CFGDesc) that matches what the generic pipeline should later produce automatically. Only then do we generalise to CFGDesc.

Execution track in progress: Finish derivative-based parsing on brzozowski. The brzozowski branch already has the derivative machinery and a regex derivative operator with soundness; the Zippy LL(1) description type is also present. Closing the existing holes and building the regex + LL(1) parsers is phases 1–3 of this plan for a narrower grammar class.

The syntactic derivative δ c G should then denote exactly ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⟜ char c, and the Brzozowski adjointness c · G ≅ δ c G is an instance of the tensor/residual adjunction char c · G ⊢ H ⟺ G ⊢ H ⟜ char c.
Why this matters for the plan:

html:ul.html:li: It grounds δ in the calculus rather than treating it as an external device: δ c G = G ⟜ char c already has the right type.
It means the parser's recursive structure can be phrased internally as currying over char c · - / uncurrying over - ⟜ char c, without leaving the calculus.
It suggests CFGDesc may not need ⟜ as a primitive — the operator can live outside the description as long as we can compute δ on descriptions and prove ⟦ δ c G ⟧cfg ≅ ⟦ G ⟧cfg ⟜ char c.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Open question: for grammars with nullable residuals the adjunction interacts with the nullability gating in δ c (G · H); make sure the semantic direction of the iso stays available in both cases. This is tracked in risks.

fr:title.text: CFGDesc: Embedded Syntax of Guarded CFGs

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: CFGDesc: Embedded Syntax of Guarded CFGs

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The first ingredient of the plan is a data type CFGDesc describing a class of grammars closed under the operations we need, for which nullability and derivatives can be computed syntactically.

Mirrors Grammar.RegularExpression.Base.RegularExpression and its denotation ⟦ _ ⟧r. The regex case is a useful template because the syntactic structure is what makes derivative-based parsing work: we can induct on the description while the semantics does not support such induction in general.
Sketch of constructors:

html:ul.html:li: ε, ⊥, char a (atoms);
_·_ (tensor), _⊕_ (alternation), _* (Kleene star);

μ (fixed points) — the CFG extension over regexes — with a productivity side condition (every self-reference must occur under a non-nullable prefix). This mirrors how the intrinsically-recursive paper uses non-nullable tensors to get a guarded list / tree functor.
⟜ and ⊸ — tentatively, to match the linear-residual derivative.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: The productivity/guardedness side condition is the syntactic counterpart of the paper's well-foundedness of the base functor. Intended denotation: ⟦ _ ⟧cfg : CFGDesc → Grammar ℓ-zero (exactly as for regexes).

The Dyck language is representable as μ D. ε ⊕ (LP · D · RP · D), where both recursive occurrences sit under non-nullable LP. This is the first concrete witness that the productivity condition admits the grammars we care about.
Downstream this tree is consumed by:

html:ul.html:li: Decidable nullability;
Syntactic derivatives;
Parser construction.

fr:title.text: Plan: Derivative-Based CFG Parser via Recursive Coalgebras

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Plan: Derivative-Based CFG Parser via Recursive Coalgebras

fr:mainmatter.html:p: A concrete path for exercising well-founded recursive coalgebras in dep-Lambek: build a generic derivative-based parser for a syntactically-delimited class of context-free grammars, in direct analogy with the existing regular-expression infrastructure (Grammar.RegularExpression). Every step should admit a compositional, well-founded account, and the whole thing should ultimately factor through the c2a-morph theorem of [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint].

The Dyck language serves as the running test: it is not regular, its derivatives form an infinite (PDA-shaped) state space, and it cannot admit a map string ⊢ Dyck — only a Parser Dyck ¬Dyck. We want to derive the automaton shape, not assume it.
The phases:

html:ol.html:li: CFGDesc: an embedded syntax of guarded CFGs.
Decidable nullability for CFGDesc.
Syntactic derivatives on CFGDesc.
Linear residual ⟜ as Brzozowski derivative.
Parser by well-founded recursion on string length.
Parser as unique c2a-morphism of a recursive coalgebra.

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Risks and open questions are tracked in sss-00AA.
An orthogonal re-foundation that would internalise phases 2 and 5 into the type system is discussed in Later operator ▶ as internalised guard.

First concrete deliverable: a hand-coded Dyck parser at the semantic level (outside CFGDesc) that matches what the generic pipeline should later produce automatically. Only then do we generalise to CFGDesc.

Execution track in progress: Finish derivative-based parsing on brzozowski. The brzozowski branch already has the derivative machinery and a regex derivative operator with soundness; the Zippy LL(1) description type is also present. Closing the existing holes and building the regex + LL(1) parsers is phases 1–3 of this plan for a narrower grammar class.

fr:title.text: Read: Intrinsically Correct Algorithms and Recursive Coalgebras

fr:frontmatter.fr:title: Read: Intrinsically Correct Algorithms and Recursive Coalgebras

fr:mainmatter.html:p: Read [alexandruIntrinsicallyCorrectAlgorithms2025-preprint] with the goal of extracting characterizations of well-founded (recursive) coalgebras that could inform the dependent Lambek calculus setting.
In particular, look for the conditions under which a coalgebra is recursive (i.e., admits unique morphisms from initial algebras) and how this is internalized in their type-theoretic framework.
